title: A leader that ignores newer terms in replies keeps serving a term the cluster has left
summary: Raft's rule for every server is one line: a message from a newer term makes you a follower. A developer narrows it for leaders, reasoning that a leader learns of a new term from the new leader's heartbeats, not from replies to its own RPCs. The behavioural contract of the role machine, 52 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in exactly one of them, and that one is the deposed-leader case.

change.description: Handle replies per role: a leader's replies only say whether its entries were accepted, so a leader no longer steps down on a reply from a newer term. Followers and candidates keep the old behaviour. The reasoning in the review was that the new leader's AppendEntries will depose the old one anyway.

risk: A leader cut off from a majority keeps sending AppendEntries. When the partition heals, the first thing it hears is the replies: followers that have moved to a newer term answer with that term, which is how Raft tells the old leader it is finished. With this change the old leader discards those replies and keeps acting as leader until a heartbeat from the new leader happens to reach it. In that window it answers reads with stale data and accepts writes it will never be able to commit, and a client that is routed to it sees a cluster with two leaders. The symptom in production is occasional stale reads after a network blip, which is close to impossible to reproduce from a bug report.
explanation: The role machine is a pure function of (role, event), and both types are finite: three roles and thirteen events (five kinds, three of them carrying a term comparison). The tool proves purity from the bytecode, executes all 52 inputs in its interpreter, and compares the outcomes with the committed contract. One case differs: `decide(LEADER, Response[term=NEWER])` used to be a transition to FOLLOWER adopting the term and is now unchanged. Nothing had to be anticipated: the contract was generated from the previous version, and the diff is the review. The state-machine view below is drawn from the patched code and shows that LEADER now has one fewer way out.
resolution: Revert. The all-servers rule is deliberately unconditional in the paper, and the role machine's contract is the right place to keep it that way: a change to any of its 52 cases is a one-line diff that a reviewer sees.
provenance: Constructed from the "Rules for Servers, All Servers" rule of the Raft paper's figure 2, by exempting leaders from it for one message kind.

references.title: Ongaro and Ousterhout, In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (figure 2, Rules for Servers)
